claims.claim: Pandora's Router decides that an expensive specialist estimate is worth paying for by computing reservation prices that quantify the expected value-of-information for querying a more accurate and costly value estimate, such as by running the specialist for a few reasoning tokens to check if it is on the right track.

The router applies value-of-information (VoI) reasoning to decide whether a posted price for a query is worth accepting and whether or not to pay to observe a refined estimate before making the final decision.

The relevant decision value for selecting an expensive specialist is the expected reward conditional on the information the router can acquire, rather than the realized downstream reward itself, which is never observed before choosing a specialist.
In practice, the learned costly estimate serves as a plug-in approximation to the posterior decision value, and the system selects the specialist for which this estimate is largest.

The router models the distribution of the costly estimate conditional on cheap estimates using a Gaussian signal model, where the mean captures the predictable component given the cheap estimates and the variance captures residual uncertainty.

The choice of the function mapping cheap estimates to the mean of the costly estimate is flexible, with implementations exploring both gradient boosted decision trees and linear regression depending on the domain.
Under a Gaussian signal model, the reservation-price-based policy derived from connecting model routing to the Pandora's Box problem has a closed form that is straightforward to compute.

passages.text: Value-based routing is a natural approach to optimizing the allocation of computing power to AI model inputs. We have argued that value estimation itself brings cost-accuracy tradeoffs, and we show how the Pandora’s Box problem offers a unified framework for value-based routing under heterogeneous value estimators. We also extend the framework to a decentralized setting, in which specialists reason about the value of information in an auction-based allocation mechanism. Limitations.Several limitations suggest promising directions for future work. The Gaussian signal model, while tractable, may not capture the heavy tails or multimodality present in some domains (see SectionD.6forcoveragestatisticsandapilotstudyofanon-Gaussiansignalmodel). Thetwo-estimator restriction (𝑓 and 𝑔) could be relaxed to chains or trees of estimators with varying performance tradeoffs. And the myopic VoI computation in the leave-one-out auction does not account for strategic anticipation of future bids; extension to a multi-round ascending-price auction (Parkes, 2005) is a natural next step. Furthermore, as discussed in Section 5, when bidding against weaker adversaries that place poor bids, Pandora’s Bidder can improve its own utility at the expense of the overall welfare.

These works establish that algorithmic design can be automated, but each demonstrates a method inside a compact search space and short proxy tasks; none is a benchmark of whether a general research agent can diagnose and improve the learning algorithm in an existing repository. Existing agent benchmarks instead score broader outcomes. MLE-Bench and MLE-Dojo reward competition submissions, while ML-Bench exercises repository-level ML tasks ; they mix data and feature engineering with model selection, hyperparameter tuning, debugging, and ensembling. Research-agent systems and benchmarks further cover idea generation, experimentation, paper writing, replication, and open-ended workshop problems , and Frontier-Eng extends executable, verifierdriven improvement to real-world engineering designs . The closest benchmarks begin with an AI system and ask an agent to improve it , but their scores aggregate gains from execution, data, capacity, hyperparameters, and learning rules; accordingly, they find tuning and engineering easier than method invention. Evenautoresearch, which opens architecture, optimizer, and training-loop code , yields edits that behave largely as hyperparameter optimization in controlled comparison . Submissions that change the learning algorithm are distinguished by modifications to the loss optimized, the supervision signal learned, the update rule itself, or the data used for training.

The gap between submissions that reach the learning algorithm layer and those that do not is attributed to the difference between the two groups rather than the effect of reaching that layer, as systems that reach it more often are stronger to begin with.

What separates submissions that reach the learning algorithm layer from those that do not is reading training dynamics as a specific failure mechanism and then addressing that mechanism, rather than just effort spent.
More reasoning effort moves agents towards changing the learning algorithm, taking the share of such submissions from 8% to 64% and increasing the mean score from 0.094 to 0.196.
The algorithmic design level is where the distance to a better algorithm is closed, and this is the layer that submissions reach least often.

passages.text: Naturalistic computer-use traces, passively recorded screenshots and mouse or keyboard actions, are a valuable resource for deriving symbolic, auditable, and reusable models of how everyday work is done. Such models matter as computer-use agents enter real work, where agents need to learn how tasks are actually performed, and organizations need to audit and reuse that knowledge. However, inducing such task models is challenging, as activity is observed only as low-level events and realworld work is multi-threaded with interleaved goals. Existing methods assume a given task or a single workflow, and produce step-level summaries rather than structured task models. We introduce TASKMODELINDUCTION(TMI), which (i) discovers the latent tasks in an unconstrained trace, disentangling concurrent activity, and (ii) for each latent task, induces a task model pairing a hierarchical objective model of recursive goal decomposition with a procedure model of the control flow that organized the execution. Intrinsically, on controlled human and agent trajectories, TMI recovers interleaved tasks with 0.974 agreement against ground-truth groupings and reconstructs 74.9% of the observed execution steps, far more than the strongest workflow induction baseline. Extrinsically, skills derived from TMI’s task models improve held-out task accuracy by 30.0% over the strongest baseline. 1
